::::

::: {.notes}

Imagine standing on a busy Melbourne street.

Trams are arriving, people are heading to work,
and pedestrians are moving in different directions.

But what happens to the same street
on a Sunday or during a lockdown?

It's the same city, but its movement changes.

That is the idea behind Pulse of Melbourne.

:::

## Flinders Street came alive after dark {#flinders-opening-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5

library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

ped <- fread(
  "../Data_pedestrians/raw/Pedestrian_Counting_System_Monthly_counts_per_hour_may_2009_to_14_dec_2022.csv",
  select = c("Year", "Month", "Mdate", "Day", "Time",
             "Sensor_ID", "Sensor_Name", "Hourly_Counts")
)

sensor_name <- "Flinders St-Elizabeth St (East)"

flinders_sat <- ped[
  Sensor_Name == sensor_name &
    Year == 2014 &
    Month == "February" &
    Day == "Saturday"
]

special_day <- flinders_sat[
  Mdate == 22,
  .(Time, Count = Hourly_Counts)
]
special_day[, Series := "22 Feb 2014"]

# Calculate the typical hourly pattern from the other Saturdays
typical_sat <- flinders_sat[
  Mdate != 22,
  .(Count = median(Hourly_Counts, na.rm = TRUE)),
  by = Time
]

typical_sat[, Series := "Other February Saturdays (median)"]

plot_data <- rbindlist(list(special_day, typical_sat))

p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(
  x = Time, y = Count,
  colour = Series, linewidth = Series
)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, by = 2)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "22 Feb 2014" = "#005EB8",
    "Other February Saturdays (median)" = "#8A8A8A"
  )) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(
    "22 Feb 2014" = 1.4,
    "Other February Saturdays (median)" = 1
  )) +
  labs(
    subtitle = "Flinders St–Elizabeth St (East)",
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Pedestrians per hour",
    colour = NULL,
    linewidth = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_blank(),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )



library(plotly)

ggplotly(
  p,
  width = 1100,
  height = 520,
  tooltip = c("x", "y", "colour")
) |>
  layout(
    hovermode = "x unified",

    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0,
      y = 1.12,
      xanchor = "left",
      yanchor = "bottom",
      font = list(size = 17)
    ),

    margin = list(
      l = 90,
      r = 30,
      t = 85,
      b = 65
    ),

    font = list(size = 18)
  ) |>
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE
  )



```

::: {.flinders-snapshot}
**FULL STUDY: 2009–2026** · **7.52 million hourly sensor observations**
:::


::: {.notes}

Let’s go back to Flinders Street on Saturday, 22 February 2014.

This graph shows pedestrian activity across the day at the Flinders Street–Elizabeth Street East sensor.

The blue line is that specific Saturday, and the grey line shows a typical Saturday in February 2014.

What stands out is that activity was noticeably higher through much of the day, especially from late morning into the evening.

So right at the beginning of our analysis, we can already see that pedestrian movement in Melbourne is not static.
It changes depending on the day, the location and what is happening in the city.

That led us to our broader question:
how does Melbourne move, and what changes its rhythm?

:::

## Beyond Flinders Street {#sensor-map-slide}

::: {.map-subtitle}
Melbourne's pedestrian sensor network
:::

```{r}
#| label: sensor-location-map
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false


library(data.table)
library(plotly)


# Official City of Melbourne sensor inventory
sensor_map <- fread(
  "figures/melbourne_sensor_locations.csv"
)

# Keep sensor IDs with valid coordinates
sensor_map <- unique(
  sensor_map[
    is.finite(latitude) &
    is.finite(longitude)
  ],
  by = "location_id"
)

setnames(
  sensor_map,
  c("latitude", "longitude"),
  c("lat", "lon")
)

# Hover information without 2025-only counts
sensor_map[, hover_text := paste0(
  "<b>", sensor_description, "</b>",
  "<br>Sensor ID: ", location_id,
  "<br>Installation date: ", installation_date
)]

# Interactive map
plot_ly(
  data = sensor_map,
  type = "scattermapbox",
  mode = "markers",
  lat = ~lat,
  lon = ~lon,
  text = ~hover_text,
  hoverinfo = "text",
  marker = list(
    size = 11,
    color = "#005EB8",
    opacity = 0.85
  ),
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  layout(
    mapbox = list(
      style = "open-street-map",
      center = list(
        lat = median(sensor_map$lat),
        lon = median(sensor_map$lon)
      ),
      zoom = 12.5
    ),
    width = 1180,
    height = 590,
    margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 0, b = 0)
  ) |>
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE,
    scrollZoom = TRUE
  )




```

::: {.sensor-snapshot}
**134 SENSOR IDs** · **INSTALLATIONS: 2009–2025** · Hover to explore
:::

::: {.notes}

We've just seen how one street in Melbourne behaved on one particular Saturday.

But Melbourne is much more than one street.

These markers show pedestrian sensor locations recorded in 2025 across the city.

Using pedestrian-counting data from the City of Melbourne, we investigated how movement varies throughout the day, across the week, between different locations and over time.

Let's begin by looking at the rhythms that shape an ordinary day in Melbourne.

:::

## Melbourne has its own daily rhythm {#daily-patterns-slide}


```{r}

#| label: daily-pedestrian-patterns
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(plotly)

# Original interactive graph — no colour changes
daily_graph <- readRDS("figures/daily_plotly.rds")

daily_graph |>
  layout(
    width = 1150,
    height = 480
  ) |>
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE
  )

```

::: {.notes}

After seeing where Melbourne's pedestrian sensors are located,
let's look at how activity changes throughout a typical day.

Pedestrian movement is not evenly distributed across 24 hours.

Activity is generally quieter overnight, increases during
the morning, and becomes much busier around lunchtime
and the late afternoon.

This shows that Melbourne has a recognisable daily rhythm.

:::

## How has Melbourne's weekly rhythm changed? {#weekly-patterns-slide}

```{r}

#| label: weekly-pedestrian-patterns
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(plotly)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

# Load weekly data covering 2009–2026
weekly_periods <- read_csv(
  "figures/weekly_periods.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# All seven days
days <- c(
  "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
  "Thursday", "Friday",
  "Saturday", "Sunday"
)

# Four periods covering the full study
periods <- c(
  "2009–2014",
  "2015–2019",
  "2020–2022",
  "2023–2026"
)

weekly_periods <- weekly_periods |>
  mutate(
    day = factor(day, levels = days),
    period = factor(period, levels = periods)
  ) |>
  arrange(period, day)

# Interactive line graph
weekly_graph <- plot_ly(
  data = weekly_periods,
  x = ~day,
  y = ~activity_index,
  color = ~period,
  colors = c(
    "2009–2014" = "#005EB8",
    "2015–2019" = "#9467BD",
    "2020–2022" = "#D97706",
    "2023–2026" = "#159A88"
  ),
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines+markers",
  line = list(width = 3),
  marker = list(size = 8),
  hovertemplate = paste0(
    "<b>%{fullData.name}</b>",
    "<br>Day: %{x}",
    "<br>Activity index: %{y:.1f}",
    "<extra></extra>"
  )
) |>
  layout(
    width = 1150,
    height = 480,

    xaxis = list(
      title = "Day of week",
      type = "category",
      categoryorder = "array",
      categoryarray = days,
      automargin = TRUE
    ),

    yaxis = list(
      title = "Activity index (100 = yearly average)",
      showgrid = TRUE,
      automargin = TRUE
    ),

    legend = list(
      orientation = "h",
      x = 0.5,
      xanchor = "center",
      y = 1.15
    ),

    font = list(size = 15),

    margin = list(
      l = 85,
      r = 65,
      t = 65,
      b = 75
    )
  ) |>
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    responsive = TRUE
  )

# Display the graph in Quarto
weekly_graph


```

::: {.notes}

We investigated how Melbourne's weekly pedestrian
rhythm has changed across the available years.

To make the changes easier to see, we summarised
2009 to 2026 into four periods.

Each line shows the relative activity pattern
from Monday to Sunday.

This allows us to examine whether the busiest
days have shifted over time, including whether
weekday and weekend activity patterns differ.

The index measures relative activity rather than
total pedestrian counts.

Because the monitoring network changes over time,
these results describe the observed network
rather than a fixed set of locations.

:::

## Has Melbourne returned to its earlier pedestrian activity? {#then-now}

::: {.tn-graphs}

::: {.tn-graph}

```{r}
#| label: slide9-daily-comparison
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

plotly::config(
  readRDS("figures/slide9_daily_plotly.rds"),
  responsive = TRUE,
  displayModeBar = FALSE
)
```

:::

::: {.tn-graph}


```{r}
#| label: slide9-hourly-comparison
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

plotly::config(
  readRDS("figures/slide9_hourly_plotly.rds"),
  responsive = TRUE,
  displayModeBar = FALSE
)
```

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
After examining long-term changes, we wanted to understand whether Melbourne had returned to its pre-pandemic pedestrian activity levels.

To make a more reliable comparison, we selected 27 sensor locations with at least 300 observed days in each of the six comparison years.

The first graph compares the median daily pedestrian count from 2017–2019 with 2023–2025.

We found a decrease from 10,091 to 7,211, which represents a 28.5% reduction.

The second graph compares hourly pedestrian activity between these periods.

Although recent pedestrian counts are generally lower, the daily rhythm remains recognisable, with activity increasing during the day and declining overnight.

This suggests that the overall level of pedestrian activity has changed more noticeably than the broad daily pattern.

These findings apply to the 27 consistently monitored locations, rather than all of Melbourne.
:::

## Where is Melbourne busiest on foot? {#spatial-pulse}

::: {.sp-bars}

```{r}
#| label: slide10-top-locations
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

plotly::config(
  readRDS("figures/slide10_top_locations_plotly.rds"),
  responsive = TRUE,
  displayModeBar = FALSE
)
```

:::

::: {.sp-method}
**2025 DATA** · Median daily pedestrian count · At least 20 hours/day and 292 valid days/location
:::

::: {.sp-takeaway}
**KEY FINDING:** Pedestrian activity varies substantially across monitored locations.
:::


::: {.notes}
We have looked at how Melbourne's pedestrian activity changes over time. Now we turn to where pedestrian activity is concentrated.

For this analysis, we focus on 2025 and compare monitored locations using their median daily pedestrian counts.

To improve reliability, we include days with at least 20 hours of observations and locations with at least 292 valid days.

The graph shows the ten busiest monitored locations meeting these criteria.

We can see that some locations record considerably higher pedestrian activity than others.

This highlights how pedestrian demand varies spatially and why planning decisions need to consider individual locations.

These rankings describe the monitored locations, rather than every street in Melbourne.
:::
